historical_timeline.summary: Resigned from the U.S. Sanitary Commission, exhausted and ill.
Chose the Belmont site for McLean Hospital.
Ceased active practice because of failing memory and vitality.
Spent a summer at a house on Deer Isle, Maine, laid out to stimulate his failing mental abilities.
Admitted to McLean Hospital, where he spent his last five years.

claims.statement: Frederick Law Olmsted was born in Hartford, Connecticut, on April 26, 1822.
Olmsted died on August 28, 1903, in Belmont, Massachusetts, at 81.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Record the death as a fact without detail.

claims.statement: Olmsted ceased active practice in 1895, a victim of failing memory and vitality; later accounts say dementia, or senility, forced his retirement, and his sons took over the firm.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the synthetic mild dementia; the retirement fixes the index year.

claims.statement: His health continued to fail after he retired. A trip to England did not help, and he became depressed there; a summer house built on Deer Isle, Maine, in 1897 was laid out to stimulate his decreasing mental abilities, but after one summer there his health continued to deteriorate.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documents the progression after the episode; claim only.

claims.statement: Olmsted, who had chosen the Belmont site of McLean Hospital in 1872, was admitted there as a patient at the end of his life and spent his last five years there, until his death in 1903.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documents the later course, after the episode; claim only.

claims.statement: His McLean Hospital medical record is sealed, and the cause of his decline is not known.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Why the record codes dementia of unspecified type.

claims.statement: Any specific type of dementia (for example Alzheimer's disease or vascular dementia) is a retrospective interpretation; the cited sources say only failing memory, senility, and dementia.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Not coded; the synthetic episode keeps the type undetermined.

claims.statement: A psychiatrist has argued retrospectively that losses in his childhood, beginning with his mother's death when he was a young child, left him with post-traumatic stress, and that his late illness made it worse.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective psychiatric interpretation; not coded and not used in the episode.

claims.statement: In 1863, exhausted and ill after overwork as head of the U.S. Sanitary Commission, Olmsted resigned.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Past history only; the illness is not specified in the cited source.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Evaluation and first-year care of progressive dementia of undetermined type in a 73-year-old man: history from the patient and an informant, MoCA, function (ADL and IADL), staging, depression screen, reversible-cause tests (vitamin B12, folate, TSH, blood count, metabolic panel) with syphilis and HIV testing only where indicated, a one-time brain MRI, disclosure of the diagnosis, a cholinesterase inhibitor trial with heart rate and side-effect checks, safety (driving, firearms, wandering, finances, home), avoidance of anticholinergic drugs, caregiver support with the Zarit Burden Interview, and advance care planning while he can take part, on the CMID non-Alzheimer's dementia and Alzheimer's disease monographs with the AAN dementia and driving parameters and the Alzheimer's Association DETeCD-ADRD guideline. Any specific cause is treated as unknown, as it is in the historical record.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Olmsted is a 73-year-old man evaluated four weeks ago for about two years of worsening memory, who returns with his caregiver for his results and is seen by behavioral neurology on the same day. Since the first visit he has stopped the glass of wine with dinner. He still repeats questions, loses track of letters and plans, and needs reminders for appointments; his caregiver now handles his medicines and bill paying. He has driven only short familiar routes, and once took a wrong turn near home this month. He sleeps well, has no hallucinations, acting out of dreams, falls, or urinary problems, and his mood is low at times when he thinks about leaving his work. The blood tests at the first visit were normal, and the brain MRI two weeks ago showed generalized and mild medial temporal atrophy with minor small-vessel change, without a stroke, tumor, or fluid build-up.

assessment_plan.assessment: Behavioral neurology confirms mild dementia (CDR 1), with IADL loss and intact basic ADL. No reversible cause was found on the blood tests, and the MRI shows no stroke, tumor, or hydrocephalus. The pattern of amnestic decline with executive difficulty and mild medial temporal atrophy fits Alzheimer's disease, but the MRI findings are not specific and no biomarker has been done, so the type remains undetermined. The diagnosis was shared with him and his caregiver, and he asked that it be explained to him plainly
plan: Start donepezil 5 mg each morning, as neurology advises, and increase to 10 mg at the three-month visit if tolerated
Stop driving now, as neurology advises; he agreed
Avoid over-the-counter sleep aids, antihistamines such as diphenhydramine, and bladder or stomach medicines with anticholinergic effects
Caregiver information on the Alzheimer's Association helpline and education programs
Advance care planning at the three-month visit, while he can take full part

hpi.narrative: Mr. Olmsted returns with his caregiver three months after his first visit, nine weeks after starting donepezil 5 mg each morning. He has had no nausea, diarrhea, loss of appetite, dizziness, fainting, or vivid dreams. His caregiver feels he is a little more engaged in the mornings, and his memory is otherwise unchanged. The night-time confusion during his cold three weeks ago stopped as soon as the diphenhydramine cold medicine was stopped, and his cough has gone. He stopped driving after the consultation and walks with company most days. He wears a medical identification bracelet. His caregiver completed the Zarit Burden Interview today and describes broken sleep, worry about leaving him alone, and little time off.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Olmsted returns with his caregiver about six months after his first visit, twelve weeks after donepezil was increased to 10 mg each morning. He has had no nausea, diarrhea, dizziness, fainting, or vivid dreams, and his appetite is good. His memory is unchanged by his caregiver's account, and he enjoys the adult day program two days a week for its gardens. He has had no falls, no wandering, and no night-time confusion. His caregiver finished the education program, sleeps better, and has two free days a week. They went through the home safety checklist together this month: knob covers on the stove, locked medicines, and night lights on the way to the bathroom.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Olmsted is a 73-year-old man with mild dementia of undetermined type (CDR 1), on donepezil 5 mg each morning for six weeks, who comes for a same-day visit with his caregiver. Five days ago he developed a runny nose and a scratchy throat, followed by a dry cough. Two nights ago, to help him sleep through the cough, his caregiver gave him an over-the-counter nighttime cold medicine containing diphenhydramine 25 mg with acetaminophen, and gave it again last night. On both nights he woke after midnight, could not find the bathroom, and was briefly unsure where he was; he settled after about half an hour with reassurance and the lights on. During the day he has been at his usual level, by his caregiver's account. He has had no fever above 37.6 °C at home, no breathlessness, no chest pain, no urinary symptoms, no falls, and no new medicines other than the cold medicine. He has not missed a donepezil dose and has had no nausea or diarrhea.

consultant_note.history: Mr. Olmsted, a 73-year-old landscape architect, is seen with his caregiver at the request of Dr. Calder for about two years of progressive memory loss. He repeats questions, loses track of correspondence and plans, and needs reminders for appointments; he stepped back from his practice this year. His caregiver now manages his medicines and bill paying. He drives short familiar routes and took a wrong turn near home this month. He has no visual hallucinations, fluctuations in alertness, acting out of dreams, tremor, falls, gait change, urinary incontinence, change in personality or social conduct, or difficulty finding words beyond names. assessment.assessment: Mild dementia (CDR global 1, FAST stage 4) rather than mild cognitive impairment, because his loss of independence in finances, medicines, and planning reflects cognitive decline. The tests have excluded thyroid disease, vitamin B12 and folate deficiency, and metabolic causes, and the MRI excludes stroke, tumor, subdural hematoma, and hydrocephalus

The gradual amnestic onset with executive difficulty and mild medial temporal atrophy fits Alzheimer's disease best, but the atrophy is within the range seen in some older adults without it, and mixed causes are common at his age. The small-vessel change is too slight to explain dementia. There are no core features of dementia with Lewy bodies, no behavioral or language features of frontotemporal dementia, and no gait or urinary features of normal pressure hydrocephalus. Without biomarkers the type cannot be established, and it is recorded as undetermined

A blood p-tau217 test, CSF, or amyloid PET could show whether Alzheimer's pathology is present, and with mild dementia he could be assessed for anti-amyloid therapy after APOE genotyping. After discussion he does not want infusions with repeated MRI monitoring and their risk of brain swelling or bleeding, and the result would not change the rest of his care. He and his caregiver chose not to test now; the option remains open
With Alzheimer's disease the most likely cause, a trial of donepezil is reasonable. His pulse is 70 with no fainting or conduction symptoms, so no ECG is needed first
At CDR 1 with a recent wrong turn, his crash risk is high, and stopping driving is advised over an on-road test. There are no firearms at home. He has not wandered
